intro/hello: Welcome to backpropagation: the algorithm that makes neural networks trainable.
intro/recall: Last chapter, we trained a classifier by walking downhill on the loss.
intro/need: Every step needs the gradient: for every weight, which way makes the loss go up, and how steeply.
intro/num: One way is numerical. Nudge one weight, run the whole loss again, and see how much it moved.
intro/slow: Simple, but slow: one extra pass per weight, and networks have millions. And only approximate, since the nudge is never truly tiny.
intro/ana: The other way is analytic: a formula from calculus. Exact and fast, but deriving it by hand for a whole network is hopeless.
intro/bp: Backpropagation is the way out. It computes exact gradients for any function, however complicated, completely mechanically.
intro/how: The trick: break the function into tiny pieces with trivial derivatives, and chain them with one rule from calculus.
intro/plan: Every deep learning library does exactly this. We will build it up from circuits with just three numbers in them.
problem/state: Let us state the problem plainly. We have a function, f, of a list of inputs, x.
problem/want: We want its gradient at one particular x: one number per input, saying how sensitive f is to that input, right there.
problem/loss: In a neural network, f is the loss: one number that says how badly the network is doing.
problem/inputs: Its inputs are the training data, and the weights.
problem/fixed: The data is given, and fixed. The weights are what we get to change.
problem/dw: So mostly, we want the gradient with respect to the weights, to step downhill.
problem/dx: The gradient on the data comes free, and is handy too, for example to see what a network has learned.
derivative/small: Start with the smallest example there is: f of x and y equals x times y.
derivative/vals: Let x be four, and y be minus three. Then f is minus twelve.
derivative/nudge: Now nudge x up a little. What happens to f?
derivative/why: f is x times minus three, so every bit you add to x takes three times as much away from f.
derivative/def: That ratio, output change per unit of input change, is the derivative.
derivative/shrink: Shrink the nudge, and the ratio settles on one exact number. Here, minus three.
derivative/sens: So a derivative is a sensitivity. Minus three means: push x up, and f moves down, three times as far.
derivative/partial: With several inputs, we ask about one input at a time, with the others frozen. That is a partial derivative, written with a curly d.
derivative/grad: The gradient is just the list of them. For x times y: y, then x. Minus three, and four.
gates/three: Three tiny functions are enough to build everything else. We just met the first.
gates/mul: For a product, the slope along x is the other input, y. And along y, it is x.
gates/mulwhy: Hold y still, and x times y is a straight line in x, with slope y.
gates/add: For a sum, the slope is always exactly one. Whatever you add to x shows up one for one in the output.
gates/max: For a max, it is all or nothing. The larger input gets a slope of one, and the smaller gets zero.
gates/maxwhy: Wiggle the smaller input a little, and nothing happens. The max does not even notice.
gates/kink: At a tie, the max has a kink with no true slope, and code just picks a side.
gates/push: Read each one as: if I push on this input, how hard does the output move?
chain/real: Real functions are built from simple pieces. Take f equals x plus y, times z.
chain/name: Name the inner piece q, equal to x plus y. Now f is q times z, and every piece is a gate we know.
chain/local: From q times z: the slope along q is z, and along z it is q. From x plus y, both slopes are one.
chain/want: But we want the slope of f along x, not along q.
chain/chain: The chain rule says how to combine the pieces: multiply them.
chain/gears: Rates multiply along a chain, like gears. x drives q at a rate of one. q drives f at minus four. So x drives f at one times minus four: minus four.
chain/calc: It is the chain rule from calculus class, outside times inside, just with actual numbers.
chain/circuit: Now draw it as a circuit: inputs on the left, one node per gate, values flowing right.
chain/fwd: Forward, left to right. x plus y gives three. Three times minus four gives minus twelve.
chain/seed: The backward pass starts at the output, with a gradient of one. Nudge f by one, and f moves by one.
chain/mulback: The multiply gate swaps its inputs. q gets z, minus four. And z gets q, three.
chain/addback: The add gate passes its minus four to both of its inputs, unchanged.
chain/result: So the gradient is minus four, minus four, and three. Nudge x a tiny bit, and f really moves by minus four times that.
chain/dx: In code we write d x. It always means the gradient of the final output with respect to x.
local/pov: Now look at the circuit from the point of view of a single gate.
local/fwd: In the forward pass, a gate gets its inputs, and computes two things from nothing but those inputs.
local/two: Its output. And its local gradients: how its output would change with each input.
local/blind: It knows nothing about the rest of the circuit: how big it is, or what it is for.
local/up: Later, the backward pass brings it one number: how much the final output cares about this gate's output. The upstream gradient.
local/rule: The chain rule says what to do with it: multiply it into each local gradient, and pass the results back to the inputs.
local/eq: Downstream equals upstream times local. That one line is the entire algorithm.
local/story: Pretend the circuit wants its output to be higher. Our add gate has local gradients of plus one, and plus one.
local/story2: Then it hears from upstream: minus four. The circuit wants its output to go down, with force four.
local/story3: So it tells both inputs: go down, with force four. If they obey, q falls, and since z is negative, f rises.
local/talk: Backprop is gates talking through gradients: should my output go up or down, and how strongly?
local/libs: Every deep learning library works this way: each layer has a forward that caches what it needs, and a backward that applies upstream times local.
local/graph: A network is a list of them: forward in order, then backward in reverse.
local/a2: Assignment two is built exactly like this, from pairs such as affine forward and affine backward.
neuron/any: Any function with a derivative we can write down can be a gate. Here is a realistic circuit: a neuron with two inputs.
neuron/formula: It takes a weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias, like a classifier's score, and squashes it between zero and one with a sigmoid.
neuron/nums: With weights two, minus three, minus three, and inputs minus one and minus two, the sum is one, and the output is about zero point seven three.
neuron/question: Which way should each weight move to push that output up? That is a backprop question.
neuron/gates: In the smallest gates, it needs four new kinds, each with a one line local gradient.
neuron/inv: One over x has a slope of minus one over x squared.
neuron/addc: Adding a constant has a slope of one. Multiplying by a constant, a, has a slope of a.
neuron/exp: And e to the x is its own derivative: its slope equals its height.
neuron/fwd: Forward first. The sum is one. Negate it, and e to the minus one is about zero point three seven. Add one, and one over that is zero point seven three.
neuron/back1: Now backward. The one over x gate turns the gradient of one into minus zero point five three.
neuron/back2: The plus one gate passes it through. The exp gate multiplies by its output, zero point three seven. And the times minus one gate flips the sign: plus zero point two.
neuron/back3: Then the add gates hand zero point two to every term, and each multiply gate swaps: w zero gets x zero times zero point two, and x zero gets w zero times it.
neuron/answer: Read off the signs. To push the output up, lower w zero and w one, and raise the bias.
sigmoid/box: Look at what those last four gates did together. They compute the sigmoid: one over one plus e to the minus z.
sigmoid/total: And between them, they scaled the gradient by about zero point one nine seven.
sigmoid/deriv: The sigmoid's derivative is unusually pleasant. Grind through the calculus, and it simplifies to one minus sigma, times sigma.
sigmoid/output: It needs only the output, which the forward pass already computed. Zero point seven three times zero point two seven is zero point one nine seven: the same factor.
sigmoid/curve: Its slope peaks at one quarter in the middle, and fades to almost nothing at both ends.
sigmoid/group: So we can swap the four small gates for one sigmoid gate, with a one line backward step.
sigmoid/modular: Grouping gates like this is common practice, whenever a group has a simple derivative.
sigmoid/code: The whole neuron is now a few lines. Forward: the dot product, then the sigmoid.
sigmoid/back: Backward: through the sigmoid, then each input gets its partner's value, times that gradient.
sigmoid/staged: Notice the habit. Split the forward pass into stages with easy derivatives, keep the values, and walk the stages backward. It is the most useful tip for writing backward passes.
staged/awkward: Here is a function made up purely for practice. Nobody would want to differentiate it by hand.
staged/page: As a formula, its derivative would take the quotient rule, the chain rule twice, and a page of algebra.
staged/value: But we never need the formula. Only its value, at our x and y: three, and minus four.
staged/stages: So break the forward pass into simple stages, and keep every intermediate value.
staged/graph: As a circuit, each stage is one gate, named after its variable.
staged/back: Then walk the stages backward. Each line is the gradient arriving from the right, times one easy local gradient.
staged/cache: Those lines need x p y, sig x and den. That is why we cache the forward pass.
staged/fork: Now watch x. It feeds three stages: sig x, x p y, and num.
staged/pieces: So its gradient arrives in three pieces, one per wire, and the pieces add up.
staged/total: One point five eight. Then one point five five. Then two point oh six.
staged/why: Nudge x, and the nudge travels down every path at once. The total effect is the sum over the paths.
staged/bug: That is why the code says plus equals. Write plain equals, and you silently drop a path: one of the most common backprop bugs.
patterns/pers: After a few circuits, the three most common gates show clear personalities on the way back.
patterns/add: The add gate distributes. It hands its upstream gradient, unchanged, to every input, whatever their values.
patterns/max: The max gate routes. The whole gradient goes to the larger input, and exactly zero to the other.
patterns/mul: The multiply gate swaps. Each input gets the other input's value, times the upstream gradient.
patterns/all: Here are all three in one circuit: two times, x times y, plus the max of z and w. Try predicting each gradient.
patterns/fwd: Forward: x times y is minus twelve. The max is two. The sum is minus ten, and doubled, minus twenty.
patterns/b1: Backward: the times two gate makes the gradient two, and the add gate distributes it: two to each side.
patterns/b2: The max routes all of it to z, since z beat w. So w gets exactly zero.
patterns/b3: And the multiply gate swaps. x gets y times two: minus eight. And y gets x times two: six.
patterns/scale: Swapping has a surprising consequence. If one input is tiny and the other is huge, the tiny one gets the huge gradient.
patterns/lin: A linear classifier multiplies weights by data. So each weight's gradient is the data value it was multiplied with.
patterns/thousand: Scale the data up a thousand times, and every weight gradient grows a thousand times, so you would need a far smaller learning rate.
patterns/pre: That is one concrete reason preprocessing matters: the size of the inputs leaks straight into the size of the gradients.
matrices/mats: So far, every value was a single number. Real networks work with whole matrices.
matrices/same: Nothing new is needed: the same rules apply, element by element. The extra care goes into shapes, and transposes.
matrices/mm: The key case is the matrix multiply. D equals W times X.
matrices/up: The upstream gradient, d D, has one number per entry of D: exactly the shape of D.
matrices/formula: The gradients are: d W equals d D times X transpose, and d X equals W transpose times d D.
matrices/why: Why? Weight W, i j, feeds every entry in row i of D, scaled by row j of X. Summing those paths gives row i of d D, dotted with row j of X.
matrices/shape: But you never need to derive that again. Use shapes. d W must have the shape of W: five by ten.
matrices/only: It is built from d D, five by three, and X, ten by three. Only one product of those comes out five by ten: d D times X transpose.
matrices/dX: Same trick for d X. W transpose, ten by five, times d D, five by three, gives ten by three: the shape of X.
matrices/sizes: Work with sizes that are all different. When two sizes match, a wrong arrangement can fit by accident.
matrices/jac: One last worry: the Jacobian, every output's derivative with respect to every input. For big vectors, it is enormous.
matrices/diag: Nobody builds it. For an element-wise operation, output i depends only on input i, so backprop just multiplies element by element.
matrices/relu: For the max of zero and x, the gradient passes wherever x was positive, and is zero everywhere else.
recap/recap: Let us put the whole algorithm together.
recap/rule: Backpropagation computes the gradient of a complicated function by applying the chain rule, over and over.
recap/fwd: Write the forward pass as simple stages, and cache their values.
recap/bwd: Then walk backward from the output, starting from a gradient of one. Each gate multiplies the upstream gradient by its local gradient, and passes it on.
recap/fork: Where a value was used more than once, its gradients add up.
recap/pers: Add distributes. Max routes. Multiply swaps.
recap/sig: A sigmoid multiplies by one minus f, times f.
recap/mat: And a matrix gradient always has the shape of its variable, which pins down the transposes.
recap/next: Next, open the interactive chapter. Every circuit you just saw is there, to step through, change, and check for yourself.
